p.x:
My name is Anna. Two years ago, my family moved from Ukraine to Thailand. I remember our departure from Kyiv. Everyone was crying. When we arrived in Bangkok, the airport was very hot! At the arrivals gate, my uncle said, "Welcome!"
At first, everything was foreign to me: the food, the language and the weather. I was the only foreigner in my class. But my classmates were very kind.
Now I have a new life here. I go to school, I have Thai friends, and I love mango sticky rice! I still miss my home country, and I think about the children I met in a camp on our journey. One day, I want to go back and visit.

Throughout history, people have moved from one place to another. Some leave behind their homes to find work or a better education; others move because they fall in love with someone from another country. Today, around 280 million people live outside the country where they were born.
Thailand is home to millions of migrants, especially from Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia. Many work in factories, on fishing boats or on building sites. To work legally, they need a work permit. Thailand also attracts many expats from Europe, America and Asia, who often work for international companies or retire here.
Moving to a new country is not easy. An immigrant must adapt to a new culture, learn a new language and find a place to live. Many say that the first year is the hardest. Over time, most people settle into their new life, although some never feel that they truly belong. Talking to a native speaker every day helps.
When you arrive in a new country, an immigration officer checks your passport and asks about your nationality. Some people emigrate permanently and eventually apply for citizenship. Others flee war or conflict and arrive as an asylum seeker, hoping to be given protection. Multicultural cities such as London, Toronto and Singapore show that diversity can make a society stronger, but sadly, racism is still a problem in many places. Some young people also go overseas to study and then return home.

Migration is one of the most debated issues of our time. For sending countries, emigration can be both a loss and a lifeline. Many lose doctors, engineers and other skilled professionals, yet the remittances that migrants send home now exceed foreign aid in many developing nations, paying for food, education and healthcare for millions of families.
For host countries, migrants often fill essential jobs. Seasonal workers harvest crops in Europe and North America, while care homes and hospitals depend heavily on foreign staff. Nevertheless, migration can provoke strong reactions. In times of economic hardship, xenophobia tends to rise, and politicians may blame newcomers for unemployment or crime, despite limited evidence.
The experience of undocumented migrants is especially difficult. Without legal status, they are vulnerable to exploitation and live in constant fear of being deported. Refugees, by contrast, are people forced to flee persecution or violence, and international law gives them the right to seek protection.
Questions of identity are complex, too. Some families choose to assimilate fully into their new society, while others maintain their language and traditions. Second-generation immigrants, born in the new country to immigrant parents, often move comfortably between two cultures, yet may feel they fully belong to neither. Many eventually travel to their parents' homeland to explore their roots. Across the world, diaspora communities have built temples, restaurants and festivals that enrich the cultures around them.
